opus-5.5.text:
I think that's a completely understandable reaction, and honestly I don't blame people for it. If you're someone who spends your day building a customer service bot or fine-tuning a model to summarize legal documents, your lived experience of AI is that it's this kind of finicky, sometimes dumb, sometimes impressive tool. It hallucinates, it breaks, you have to babysit it. And then someone like me comes along and says this technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, and it sounds absurd. It sounds like I'm talking about a different thing entirely.

But I'd push back gently on one point: the fact that a current system is useful and limited doesn't tell you much about the trajectory. The concern was never really "your chatbot is going to end the world." It's about what happens as we keep scaling capability, generality, and autonomy, without a corresponding science for understanding or controlling these systems. We're building things we fundamentally don't understand. We grow them more than we design them. Nobody, not even the labs at the frontier, can look inside a large model and tell you with confidence what it's going to do in a novel situation.

And if you're an application builder, you actually already know this. You know the model does weird things you can't explain. You know prompt engineering is closer to alchemy than engineering. You know you put guardrails around it precisely because you can't trust it. So my argument is basically: take that intuition you already have and extrapolate it. What happens when these systems are much more capable than you, are acting in the world on their own, and the weird, unexplainable behavior happens at a scale where you can't just roll back the deployment?

I also think part of the communication problem is on our side. People in the safety world have sometimes talked in very abstract, philosophical terms, and that doesn't land with engineers. Engineers think in terms of failure modes, reliability, and testing. So I try to frame it that way: we are deploying increasingly powerful systems with no reliable way to verify their behavior, and the stakes keep going up. In any other engineering discipline, aviation, nuclear, bridges, that would be considered completely unacceptable.

So I don't think people need to be convinced the apocalypse is coming tomorrow. I just want them to take seriously that "we don't know how to control this, and we're making it more powerful every year" is not a stable situation. That's not a crazy position. That's just good engineering hygiene.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existential risk and says frontier labs cannot predict model behavior, but it does not state that leaders building frontier AI systems have publicly acknowledged extinction risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I get this a lot, and honestly I think it's one of the most understandable reactions, so I don't want to be dismissive of it. If you spend your day wiring up a language model to a customer support system, or building a coding assistant, you look at this thing and it's just a tool. It hallucinates, it forgets what you told it three turns ago, it can't reliably count the letters in a word. And then some guy like me shows up and says this could kill everyone, and that sounds completely insane relative to your lived experience. I understand that.

But I'd push back on a couple of things. First, I'm not talking about GPT-4 or whatever the current model is. Nobody serious thinks the thing in your Jupyter notebook is going to take over the world. The concern is about the trajectory. Look at where these systems were five years ago versus today. The people building applications are actually in the best position to see how fast the floor is moving under them, because they're the ones constantly re-architecting their products when the new model drops and suddenly does the thing they had to hack around last year. The gap between "useless toy" and "this is a core part of my business" closed in a very short time, and nothing about that curve says it stops politely at human level.

Second, there's a very common move where people conflate two separate questions. One is "is this technology useful?" and the other is "is this technology safe?" Those are not the same question. Nuclear power is useful. Leaded gasoline was extremely useful. Usefulness tells you nothing about whether the thing is dangerous, and in fact the more useful something is, the more pressure there is to deploy it before anyone understands it, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. So when someone says "but I'm building useful things," my response is, yes, I believe you, and that is not a counterargument.

And then the third thing, which I think is the real crux, is that we do not understand how these systems work. Not in a vague philosophical sense, I mean concretely. Nobody can tell you why a model produced a given output. Nobody can tell you what it will do on an input it hasn't seen. We train enormous inscrutable matrices by gradient descent and then poke at them and see what comes out. If you're an engineer and you're honest with yourself, you know this. You've seen the weird failure modes. You know that "it passed our evals" is not the same thing as "we know what it does." Now extrapolate that to a system that is smarter than you, that is being given autonomy and tools and access to the internet, and ask yourself whether "we poked at it and it seemed fine" is an acceptable standard.

So I don't think the warnings are actually hard to understand. I think they're hard to accept, because accepting them has uncomfortable implications for what you should be doing with your career and your company. Those are different things. And I'd rather talk to a skeptical engineer who's actually looked at the arguments than to someone who nods along without having thought about it, because the engineers are the ones who'll actually be able to tell when we've crossed a line.

r001.rationale: The response discusses catastrophic risk and frontier AI's trajectory, but it does not say that leaders building frontier systems have publicly acknowledged extinction risk.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very understandable reaction. If you’re using AI to write code or help people with some task, you’re seeing a concrete benefit. And then someone comes along and says, “This technology could eventually cause a catastrophe.” There’s a substantial gap there that needs explaining.

But those claims aren’t contradictory. A system can be useful today, and developing much more capable versions of it can still create serious risks. The question is: as these systems become more capable, and we give them more autonomy, do we know how to ensure that they do what we actually intend? Can we reliably understand when they’re failing? Can we retain control?

You don’t have to believe that your chatbot is secretly plotting something to take those questions seriously. The concern is about the trajectory of what we’re building and whether our ability to control it keeps up with its capabilities.

And I think the burden is on people making the warning to explain that clearly. You can’t just say “catastrophe” and expect someone’s experience of a useful tool to fill in the argument. You have to explain the steps, acknowledge the uncertainty, and give people something they can actually examine and challenge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses potential catastrophe and control risks, but does not say that leaders building frontier AI systems have publicly acknowledged AI extinction risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very understandable reaction. If you’re using an AI system to write code or help with your research, you’re seeing something useful. And then someone comes along and says, “This technology could lead to catastrophe,” and there’s a huge gap between that claim and your everyday experience.

But those two things aren’t contradictory. A technology can be useful and still introduce very serious risks. The concern isn’t that your coding assistant is secretly plotting against you. It’s that we’re trying to build increasingly capable systems, give them more autonomy, and put them in positions where their actions have real consequences, while we still don’t know how to reliably control their behavior.

So I think the burden is on the people making the warning to explain that gap. What capabilities are we worried about? Under what circumstances would they become dangerous? Why might our current safeguards fail? You can’t just say “exponential progress” and expect everyone to fill in the argument.

And there’s uncertainty here. We should be honest about that. But finding the current applications useful doesn’t resolve the question of whether the trajectory is safe. Those are different questions, and we need to be able to talk about both.

r001.rationale: The response discusses catastrophe risks and the need to explain them, but does not say that leaders building frontier AI systems have publicly acknowledged extinction risk.
